opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way we've used computers for the last few decades has been shaped by the limits of what computers could do. You had to go to the computer, open an app, click through menus, and translate what you wanted into something the machine understood. That made sense when software was dumb.

But now the software can actually understand you. It can reason, hold context, and take actions on your behalf. When that's true, a lot of the old interface assumptions start to feel strange. Why am I juggling fifty apps and tabs, getting interrupted by notifications all day, when what I want is something that knows what I'm trying to do and helps me get it done?

So the question we keep asking is: what does a computer look like if it's designed from the ground up for AI? I think it's something more ambient, more aware of your context, and much calmer. Less like a slot machine fighting for your attention, more like a trusted assistant who's with you, understands what you care about, and only gets in your way when it matters.

There's a hardware piece to that, and there's a software and model piece. Honestly, the models are getting good enough that the bottleneck is starting to be the form factor and the interface, not the intelligence. That's exciting, because it means there's room for a genuinely new kind of device, not just a better version of the phone or laptop.

I don't think the old devices go away. People will still have phones and laptops for a long time. But I do think there's a new category to build, and it's one of the things I'm most excited about. It's hard, and we'll probably get some things wrong at first, but the opportunity to rethink how people relate to computers doesn't come around very often.

r001.rationale: It says today’s computer use was shaped by computers’ limits and that old interface assumptions made sense when software was “dumb.”

r002.rationale: It describes an AI-era computer as “aware of your context” and able to understand what the user is trying to do.

r003.rationale: It describes ambient assistance and AI taking actions, but does not clearly say interaction should extend beyond typing and looking at a screen.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss meeting information or the AI judging which information it may share with particular people.

r005.rationale: It mentions helping and taking actions on the user’s behalf, but not delegating appropriate follow-up actions through a single question based on trust in the AI’s judgment.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know yet, and I find that exciting rather than frustrating. The computers we use today were designed for a world without AI. The phone, the laptop, the whole paradigm of windows and apps and typing and tapping, that all assumes you are the one doing the work and the computer is a tool you operate. I think that assumption is about to break.

If you have something that actually understands you, that has context on your life, that can take actions on your behalf, then the right interface probably looks very different. You shouldn't have to pull a device out of your pocket, unlock it, find an app, and translate what you want into a sequence of taps. The computer should just be there, aware of what's going on, and mostly quiet. It should interrupt you rarely and only when it matters, and it should be able to do a lot in the background without you supervising every step.

So when we think about what to build, we start from the question of what a relationship with a computer looks like when the computer is smart. I think it's less like a tool and more like a very capable collaborator. That has implications for the hardware, sure, but honestly the hardware is the less interesting part. The interesting part is the software layer, the model that knows you, that remembers, that can see and hear and act across everything you do. The form factor follows from that.

I'd also say, and I believe this strongly, that it should be calm. The devices of the last fifteen years have been incredibly good at capturing attention, and I don't think that was a great trade for people. If we do this right, the AI computer should give you back time and attention rather than take it. That's a design principle, not just a nice sentiment, and it's one we'll be judged on.

We're still early. It'll take a few iterations, and some of what we try won't work. But I think the first truly new kind of computer in decades is a real possibility, and it's one of the things I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: It says today’s computers were designed for a world without AI.

r002.rationale: It describes a computer with context on the user’s life that knows and remembers them.

r003.rationale: It contrasts typing and tapping with an AI that can see, hear, and act across what the user does.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss meetings or the AI’s permission to share meeting information with particular people.

r005.rationale: It mentions actions on the user’s behalf, but does not connect trust in the AI’s judgment to delegating appropriate follow-up actions through a single question.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is: what should a computer look like when it can actually understand what you’re trying to do? We’re used to computers where you open an application, find the right menu, and tell it exactly what to do, step by step. With AI, you can start with the intent: here’s what I’m trying to accomplish. And the computer can help figure out the steps with you.

That makes me think there’s an opportunity to rethink the whole experience, rather than just put a chat window inside everything. You’d want something that understands the relevant context of your life, that can help across different tasks, and that knows when to act and when to ask. Getting that last part right is really important. You should feel like you have more control and more ability, even as you spend less time operating the computer.

I don’t think the final form of that is obvious yet. But a computer that adapts to you, instead of requiring you to learn how to use it—that’s a pretty exciting direction.

r001.rationale: It describes the familiar application-and-menu workflow and contrasts it with AI, but does not identify current computer design as reflecting a world without AI.

r002.rationale: It says an AI-era computer should understand relevant context of a user's life.

r003.rationale: It discusses intent-based interaction and chat, but does not suggest interaction beyond typing and looking at a screen.

r004.rationale: It does not mention meetings or deciding what information may be shared with particular people.

r005.rationale: It says the computer should know when to act or ask, but does not describe delegating follow-up actions through a single question based on trust in the AI's judgment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is what a computer looks like when it can understand what you’re trying to do, rather than requiring you to translate everything into a series of clicks and commands. We’ve gotten very used to working around the computer. With AI, there’s an opportunity for the computer to do more of that work for us.

You should be able to describe an intention, have a conversation when something needs clarification, and trust the system to help carry it through. Sometimes that calls for a screen and a keyboard. Sometimes you’d rather just say something and get on with your day.

But I don’t think we know the final form yet. The thing to aim for is something that gives people more capability while demanding less of their attention—and keeps them in control of what it does.

r001.rationale: The response says current computers require clicks and commands, but does not clearly identify their design as reflecting a world without AI.

r002.rationale: It says a computer should understand what the user is trying to do, but does not describe awareness of the broader context of the user's life.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says some interactions could happen by speaking rather than using a screen and keyboard.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss meeting information or permissions for sharing it with particular people.

r005.rationale: It mentions trusting the system to carry out an intention, but not delegating appropriate follow-up actions through a single question.
